1. Convolution

The notion of convolution is so fundamental in Fourier analysis and in applications (guess anyone hasn't heard of the convolutional neural network?). We have seen its appearance last time: that the symmetric partial sum of the Fourier series of a (say) continuous function f:[0,2π]→C {f:[0,2\pi]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}}f:[0,2π]→C is obtained by convolving f {f}f with the Dirichlet kernel

∑∣n∣≤Nf^(n)einθ=f∗DN  (θ).\displaystyle \sum_{|n|\leq N}\hat{f}(n)e^{in\theta}=f*D_{N}\;(\theta).∣n∣≤N∑​f^​(n)einθ=f∗DN​(θ).

And the solution to the Laplace equation on the unit disk is obtained by convolving the given boundary value u0:S1≡∂B(0,1)→C {u_{0}:S^{1}\equiv\partial B(0,1)\rightarrow\mathbb{C}}u0​:S1≡∂B(0,1)→C with the Poisson kernel

u(r,θ)=u0∗Pr  (θ),0<r<1.\displaystyle u(r,\theta)=u_{0}*P_{r}\;(\theta),\quad0<r<1.u(r,θ)=u0​∗Pr​(θ),0<r<1.

In this post we aim to grasp some basic properties of convolution in the context of Fourier series.
First, let us address again our objects of study. There are three basically equivalent categories

  • Functions defined on [0,2π] {[0,2\pi]}[0,2π];
  • Functions defined on the circle S1 {S^{1}}S1;
  • 2π {2\pi}2π-periodic functions defined on R {\mathbb{R}}R;

For the first class of functions, we have the agreement that values of the function at the endpoints are not important for computing Fourier coefficient, and thus can be made equivalent to the following two classes by possibly altering the function's value at the endpoints (which may not be continuous anymore, but remains integrable). The second class of functions can easily be 2π {2\pi}2π-periodically extended to the real line. In the context of Fourier series, convolution of two functions is indispensable with the periodicity of the functions. This is manifested in the following definition.

Definition 1 (Convolution of two 2π {2\pi}2π-periodic functions) For two continuous, 2π {2\pi}2π-periodic functions f,g:R→C {f,g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}}f,g:R→C, their convolution is again a 2π {2\pi}2π-periodic function, defined to be
f∗g  (x)=∫[0,2π]f(y)g(x−y)  dy\displaystyle f*g\;(x)=\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(y)g(x-y)\;dyf∗g(x)=∫[0,2π]​f(y)g(x−y)dy

Exercise 1 Check that for the same f,g {f,g}f,g as above,

f∗g  (x)=∫[0,2π]f(x−y)g(y)  dy=g∗f  (x).\displaystyle f*g\;(x)=\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(x-y)g(y)\;dy=g*f\;(x).f∗g(x)=∫[0,2π]​f(x−y)g(y)dy=g∗f(x).

One can think of convolution f∗g  (x) {f*g\;(x)}f∗g(x) as a g {g}g-weighted averaged version of f {f}f, or equivalently one can think of it as an f {f}f-weighted averaged version of g {g}g, which interpretation is more sensible depends on the context. The weight function is usually called a kernel. For example, we would say the interior of the solution u(r,θ) {u(r,\theta)}u(r,θ) to the Laplace equation is obtained by averaging the boundary value u0 {u_{0}}u0​ with the Poisson kernel Pr {P_{r}}Pr​.

We gather some basic properties of convolution below.

  • (f∗g)∗h=f∗(g∗h) {(f*g)*h=f*(g*h)}(f∗g)∗h=f∗(g∗h).*

The relation between convolution and Fourier coefficient is contained in the next proposition.

Proposition 1 Suppose f,g:R→C {f,g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}}f,g:R→C are continuous and 2π {2\pi}2π-periodic. Then

f∗g^(n)=2πf^(n)g^(n).\displaystyle \widehat{f*g}(n)=2\pi\hat{f}(n)\hat{g}(n).f∗g​(n)=2πf^​(n)g^​(n).

Proof: The result can be proved directly by writing out

f∗g^(n)=12π∫[0,2π](∫[0,2π]f(x−y)g(y)dy)e−inxdx=∫[0,2π](12π∫[−y,2π−y]f(x−y)e−in(x−y)g(y)e−inyd(x−y))dy=∫[0,2π]f^(n)g(y)e−inydy=2πf^(n)g^(n).\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} \widehat{f*g}(n) & = & \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}\left(\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(x-y)g(y)dy\right)e^{-inx}dx\\ & = & \int_{[0,2\pi]}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[-y,2\pi-y]}f(x-y)e^{-in(x-y)}g(y)e^{-iny}d(x-y)\right)dy\\ & = & \int_{[0,2\pi]}\hat{f}(n)g(y)e^{-iny}dy\\ & = & 2\pi\hat{f}(n)\hat{g}(n). \end{array}f∗g​(n)​====​2π1​∫[0,2π]​(∫[0,2π]​f(x−y)g(y)dy)e−inxdx∫[0,2π]​(2π1​∫[−y,2π−y]​f(x−y)e−in(x−y)g(y)e−inyd(x−y))dy∫[0,2π]​f^​(n)g(y)e−inydy2πf^​(n)g^​(n).​

In the second step we have interchanged the integral and made a change of variable. Using the fact that f(x) {f(x)}f(x) and einx {e^{inx}}einx are 2π {2\pi}2π-periodic, so that the integral gives f^(n) {\hat{f}(n)}f^​(n). □ \Box□

Exercise 3 What are the Fourier coefficients of f∗DN  (θ) {f*D_{N}\;(\theta)}f∗DN​(θ), where DN {D_{N}}DN​ is the N {N}N-th Dirichlet kernel? What are the Fourier coefficients of f∗Pr  (θ) {f*P_{r}\;(\theta)}f∗Pr​(θ), where Pr {P_{r}}Pr​ is the Poisson kernel with radius r {r}r, 0<r<1 {0<r<1}0<r<1? Plot the Fourier coefficients of DN {D_{N}}DN​ and Pr {P_{r}}Pr​, and how are they different?

The above relation can be interpreted this way: as we have shown in Exercise 2, the mapping f↦f∗g {f\mapsto f*g}f↦f∗g is linear, and in analogy to matrices we can think of it as

f↦Gf\displaystyle f\mapsto Gff↦Gf

for some matrix G {G}G. Expressing these function under Fourier series, we find the very same mapping expressed in Fourier coefficients is

f^(n)↦2πg^(n)f^(n)\displaystyle \hat{f}(n)\mapsto2\pi\hat{g}(n)\hat{f}(n)f^​(n)↦2πg^​(n)f^​(n)

or equivalently, in matrix form

f^=(⋮f^(1)f^(2)f^(3)⋮)↦2π(⋱g^(1)g^(2)g^(3)⋱)(⋮f^(1)f^(2)f^(3)⋮)\displaystyle \hat{f}=\begin{pmatrix}\vdots\\ \hat{f}(1)\\ \hat{f}(2)\\ \hat{f}(3)\\ \vdots \end{pmatrix}\mapsto2\pi\begin{pmatrix}\ddots\\ & \hat{g}(1)\\ & & \hat{g}(2)\\ & & & \hat{g}(3)\\ & & & & \ddots \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\vdots\\ \hat{f}(1)\\ \hat{f}(2)\\ \hat{f}(3)\\ \vdots \end{pmatrix}f^​=​⋮f^​(1)f^​(2)f^​(3)⋮​​↦2π​⋱​g^​(1)​g^​(2)​g^​(3)​⋱​​​⋮f^​(1)f^​(2)f^​(3)⋮​​

in other words, the under the Fourier basis, the convolution is diagonalized! This will happen exactly the same for the discrete Fourier transform.
We have seen that under the Fourier basis the differential operator is also diagonalized. For completeness we record this result.

Remark 1 In fact, differentiation can also be represented as a convolution! (But to describe the kernel will be out of scope). In any case, the above diagonalization result can be seen as a special instance of a generalized version of Proposition 1.

Remark 2 Let us suppose we have a nice 2π2\pi2π-periodic continuous function whose Fourier series converges to the function itself, i.e. u0(θ)=∑n∈Zu0^(n)einθ,u_{0}(\theta) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\hat{u_{0}}(n)e^{in\theta},u0​(θ)=∑n∈Z​u0​^​(n)einθ, and we set it to be the initial value of the heat equation. In addition if we think of this function to be defined on the circle, then there will be no boundary conditions. Then we can find that the solution to the heat equation is then u(t,θ)=∑n∈Ze−tn2u0^(n)einθ.u(t,\theta) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-tn^2}\hat{u_{0}}(n)e^{in\theta}.u(t,θ)=∑n∈Z​e−tn2u0​^​(n)einθ. Compare this expression with the solution to the Laplace equation. You can recognize it as obtained by convolution with certain function, which is known as the heat kernel. You may also want to compare the Fourier coefficients of the heat kernel with those of the Dirichlet and Poisson kernel.
